questions.correct_answer: It proves a language is non-regular by showing that for every pumping length p there is some string in L that cannot be pumped; it cannot by itself prove a language is regular.
questions.explanation: The pumping lemma is a necessary condition for regularity, so it is used contrapositively to prove non-regularity: you must show that for every p some string fails every valid decomposition. Pumping success on some strings never proves regularity, and a single pumpable decomposition does not rule out non-regularity.
options: It proves a language is non-regular by showing that for every pumping length p there is some string in L that cannot be pumped; it cannot by itself prove a language is regular.
It proves a language is regular if every string in L of length at least p can be pumped.
It proves a language is regular if at least one string in L of length at least p can be pumped.
It proves a language is non-regular if some string in L can be pumped with a particular decomposition.
questions.question: Which statement correctly describes what the pumping lemma for regular languages can and cannot establish?

questions.correct_answer: EQ_DFA = {<A, B> : A and B are DFAs and L(A) = L(B)}
questions.explanation: EQ_DFA is decidable because the symmetric difference of two DFA languages is regular and emptiness of a DFA is checkable, so you can test whether it is empty. A_TM is undecidable (it is recognizable but not decidable), E_TM and EQ_TM are undecidable by Rice's theorem since they concern nontrivial properties of the language of a Turing machine.
options: A_TM = {<M, w> : M is a Turing machine that accepts input w}
E_TM = {<M> : M is a Turing machine and L(M) = ∅}
EQ_TM = {<M1, M2> : M1 and M2 are Turing machines and L(M1) = L(M2)}
EQ_DFA = {<A, B> : A and B are DFAs and L(A) = L(B)}
